# DLA Piper welcomes David Cameron, former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, as consultant

* [Background](https://iberianlawyer.com/category/background/)
* 09/06/2025
* 507
* 2 minutes read

**David Cameron** , former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, has joined global law firm **[DLA Piper](https://iberianlawyer.com/?s=DLA+Piper)** as a consultant. He will provide guidance on the various geographies in which the firm operates, including on the issue of geopolitical risk.

**Charles Severs** , Global Co-CEO at DLA Piper, added: “Lord Cameron’s vast experience in global leadership and policymaking will be a tremendous asset to our leadership team. His insights will significantly enhance our ability to deliver exceptional legal services to our clients worldwide.”

## **David Cameron**
Lord Cameron has a wealth of experience, having served as Prime Minister of the UK from 2010 to 2016 and, more recently, as the UK’s Foreign Secretary from 2023 to 2024. Beyond politics, he contributes to global thought leadership as a member of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Global Board of Advisors and as a Visiting Professor at New York University Abu Dhabi.

“Lord Cameron brings a unique perspective to advising the firm on the evolving global landscape,” said **Frank Ryan** , DLA Piper’s Global Co-CEO. “His appointment as Consultant further positions us to counsel clients on navigating challenges and seizing opportunity wherever they do business.”

[[ 86 ]]() In 1902, for example, Arthur Balfour said, "The prime minister has no salary as prime minister. He has no statutory duties as prime minister, his name occurs in no Acts of Parliament, and though holding the most important place in the constitutional hierarchy, he has no place which is recognized by the laws of his country. This is a strange paradox". Despite its growing dominance in the constitutional hierarchy, the premiership was given little formal recognition until the 20th century; the [legal fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_fiction "Legal fiction") was maintained that the sovereign still governed directly.

Also important would be the question of who was likely to be in contention to take over long-term as Prime Minister. If the most senior member of the Government was him or herself a contender for the role of Prime Minister, it might be that The Queen would invite a slightly less senior non-contender. In these circumstances, her private secretary would probably take soundings, via the Cabinet Secretary, of members of the Cabinet, to ensure that The Queen invited someone who would be acceptable to the Cabinet to act as their chair during the caretaker period. Once the Party had elected a new leader, that person would, of course, be invited to take over as Prime Minister.

Public recognition of the existence of a 'Prime Minister's Office' in the Civil Service Yearbook came as recently as the 1977 edition. [[ 37 ]]()

The prime minister is customarily a member of the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_the_United_Kingdom "Privy Council of the United Kingdom") and thus entitled to the appellation " [The Right Honourable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Right_Honourable "The Right Honourable") ". Membership of the Council is retained for life. It is a constitutional convention that only a privy counsellor can be appointed prime minister. Most potential candidates have already attained this status.

...

The honour bestowed is commonly, but not invariably, membership of the UK's most senior order of chivalry, the [Order of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Garter "Order of the Garter") . The practice of creating a retired prime minister a Knight Companion of the Garter (KG) has been fairly prevalent since the mid-nineteenth century. Upon the retirement of a prime minister who is Scottish, it is likely that the primarily Scottish honour of [Knight of the Thistle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Thistle "Order of the Thistle") (KT) will be used instead of the Order of the Garter, which is generally regarded as an English honour. [[ n 5 ]]()

Historically it has also been common to grant prime ministers a [peerage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peerage "Peerage") upon retirement from the Commons, elevating the individual to the Lords. Formerly, the peerage bestowed was usually an [earldom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl "Earl") .

...

The most recent former prime minister to die was Margaret Thatcher (1979–1990) on 8 April 2013. Her death meant that for the first time since 1955 (the year in which the [Earldom of Attlee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earldom_of_Attlee "Earldom of Attlee") was created, subsequent to the death of [Earl Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Baldwin_of_Bewdley "Earl Baldwin of Bewdley") in 1947) the membership of the House of Lords included no former prime minister, a situation which remained the case until David Cameron was appointed to the House in November 2023.

### Activities
There are currently no established roles or job positions for former prime ministers following their resignations or after leaving office unexpectedly. It depends on their personal choice and reasons surrounding the need to take on such positions. During the 18th and 19th centuries, many former prime ministers, who were wealthy members of the [nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_nobility "British nobility") , would often simply retire to their country estates. The first prime minister, [Robert Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Walpole "Robert Walpole") , accumulated large personal wealth while serving in office and from previous investments made in the 1710s. Prime ministers [Lord Bute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stuart,_3rd_Earl_of_Bute "John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute") and [Lord Rosebery](https://en.wikipedia.

However, some former prime ministers have returned to serve in the governments of their successors, and a few have had 'retreads' that saw them serve short tenures due to their successors unexpectedly resigning or dying. Notable cases include the [Duke of Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington "Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington") who, after serving two brief terms in office, was able to command significant influence as a senior member of the [Tory party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tories_\(British_political_party\) "Tories (British political party)") and returned to serve in two governments of his successor, [Robert Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Peel "Robert Peel") , as [Foreign Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Secretary_\(United_Kingdom\) "Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)") and [Minister without portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.

[Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home") , who resigned after losing the [1964 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_Kingdom_general_election "1964 United Kingdom general election") , later came to serve in the cabinet of Edward Heath in 1970. [[ 165 ]]() [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") returned 7 years after [resigning as Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath_of_the_2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "Aftermath of the 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum") to serve as Foreign Secretary under [Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak "Rishi Sunak") . [[ 166 ]]()

### Public Duty Costs Allowance (PDCA)

All former prime ministers are entitled to claim for salary or office expenses incurred in fulfilling public duties in that role.
The allowance may not be used to pay for private or parliamentary duties. It is administered by the Cabinet Office Finance Team.

The maximum amount which may be claimed per year is £115,000, plus 10% towards any staff pension costs. This limit is reviewed annually, and at the start of each Parliament, by the current prime minister. The maximum level may be adjusted downward if the former prime minister receives any public funds for fulfilling other public appointments. [[ 167 ]]() Downing Street confirmed in November 2023 that former prime minister David Cameron would not claim from the PDCA [while he acted as Foreign Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron's_tenure_as_Foreign_Secretary "David Cameron's tenure as Foreign Secretary") . [[ 168 ]]()

# Living prime ministers of the United Kingdom

From EverybodyWiki Bios & Wiki

Jump to: navigation , search

This is a chronological list of all those who served as British prime minister and were still living at different periods in history. Currently, there are nine living prime ministers: John Major , Tony Blair , Gordon Brown , David Cameron , Theresa May , Boris Johnson , Liz Truss , Rishi Sunak , and Keir Starmer .
There have been four periods when there was only one living prime minister, starting with the appointment (1721) of Robert Walpole , and most recently during the second term of William Ewart Gladstone upon the death (1881) of Benjamin Disraeli .

There has been one time period when nine living current or former prime ministers co-existed. This period has been ongoing since July 2024, when Keir Starmer was appointed prime minister; his eight living predecessors are John Major , Tony Blair , Gordon Brown , David Cameron , Theresa May , Boris Johnson , Liz Truss , and Rishi Sunak .

There have been eleven periods when six living current or former prime ministers co-existed which was the previous record number of living prime ministers prior to the appointment of Liz Truss , [[ lower-alpha 1 ]]() with the longest being a nine-year period beginning with the first appointment (1834) of Robert Peel .
The most recent period was from July 2019 to September 2022, when Boris Johnson was appointed prime minister; his five living predecessors were John Major , Tony Blair , Gordon Brown , David Cameron , and Theresa May . There has been one period (1754) with no living prime minister, a period of ten days that spanned the death of Henry Pelham on 6 March and the appointment of the Duke of Newcastle . [[ lower-alpha 2 ]]()

If one were to include future prime ministers, there was one period when nineteen had co-existed (See § [# [§ Statistics , below| § Statistics , below]], below.) .

## Current living prime ministers

Living prime ministers as of August 3, 2026 ( _from oldest to youngest_ ):

* There have been four men who have been the only living prime minister: Robert Walpole (as the first, from April 1721 to February 1742), Henry Pelham (from Walpole's death in March 1745 to March 1754), Duke of Newcastle (from Newcastle's appointment in March 1754 to November 1756) and William Ewart Gladstone (from Benjamin Disraeli 's death in April 1881 to June 1885).
* During one period in the history of the United Kingdom , has there been nine persons alive to have been prime minister. This period has been ongoing since 5 July 2024 (with John Major , Tony Blair , Gordon Brown , David Cameron , Theresa May , Boris Johnson , Liz Truss , Rishi Sunak , and Keir Starmer as the living prime ministers).
* During eleven periods in the history of Great Britain and the United Kingdom from 1801 to present, have there been six persons alive to have been prime minister, which was the previous record number of living prime ministers prior to the appointment of Liz Truss on 5 September 2022.

...

Asquith , David Lloyd George , Stanley Baldwin , and Ramsay MacDonald were alive); from 16 October 1964 to 24 January 1965 (when Winston Churchill , Clement Attlee , Anthony Eden , Harold Macmillan , Alec Douglas-Home , and Harold Wilson were alive); from 5 April 1976 to 14 January 1977 (when Anthony Eden , Harold Macmillan , Alec Douglas-Home , Harold Wilson , Edward Heath , and James Callaghan were alive); from 4 May 1979 to 29 December 1986 (when Harold Macmillan , Alec Douglas-Home , Harold Wilson , Edward Heath , James Callaghan , and Margaret Thatcher were alive); from 28 November 1990 to 24 May 1995 (when Alec Douglas-Home , Harold Wilson , Edward Heath , James Callaghan , Margaret Thatcher , and John Major were alive). The eleventh and most recent period was from 24 July 2019 to 5 September 2022 (with John Major , Tony Blair , Gordon Brown , David Cameron , Theresa May , and Boris Johnson as the living prime ministers).
Of these periods, the earliest two and the most recent three consisted of each prime minister appointed consecutively. The longest period where there have been six living prime ministers was 9 years and 67 days, ending with the death of Addington in February 1844.
* There has been only one period where there has been no living prime minister – in March 1754 following Pelham's death on 6 March to Newcastle's appointment on 16 March.
* Duke of Newcastle was the only person to be both the only living prime minister (from 16 March 1754 to 16 November 1756) and one of six or more living prime ministers (from 14 October to 17 November 1768).
* John Major and Tony Blair are the only persons to have been one of three or less living prime ministers (from 17 July 2005 to 27 June 2007) and one of the nine living prime ministers (from 5 July 2024 to present).
* There have been 25 administrations during which a prime minister has not died, the most recent being the administration of Rishi Sunak .
This does not include the administrations of Earl of Wilmington , Marquess of Rockingham , and George Canning (who were themselves the only prime ministers to die during their administrations), nor the administration of incumbent Keir Starmer (as no prime minister has died since Margaret Thatcher , who died during the administration of David Cameron . Conversely, only twice (during the administrations of William Pitt the Younger and Stanley Baldwin ) has there been as many as three deaths during a premiership. (This does not include the administration of Spencer Perceval 's administration, whose own death]] was the third during his term). The longest streak of administrations without a prime ministerial death is four: no prime minister died during the administrations of Theresa May , Boris Johnson , Liz Truss , or Rishi Sunak (this would increase to five if no prime minister dies during Keir Starmer 's administration.
If one were to include the multiple terms served by each prime minister that had been in office more than once, the record is five: no prime minister died during Salisbury 's first term, Gladstone 's third term, Salisbury 's second term, Gladstone 's fourth term or during the term of Rosebery .
* Because he was the first prime minister, and the fact that he's also the longest serving serving prime minister, Robert Walpole holds the distinction of serving for the longest period during which no prime ministers died. The second longest term without a death of a prime minister would be that of Earl of Liverpool who served almost fifteen years in office. In recent years, the prime minister who served the longest without a death during his term was Harold Macmillan , who served for almost seven years in office.
* The longest period between deaths of prime ministers was the 17 years and 41 days between the deaths of Stanley Baldwin on 14 December 1947 and Winston Churchill on 24 January 1965.

...

In modern times, the prime minister to have lived to see the most administrations following their own was David Lloyd George , with eight following the end of his administration in 1922.
* If one includes future as well as past and current prime ministers, the record sits at nineteen:
  
    + Between Disraeli 's birth on 21 December 1804 and Shelburne 's death on 7 May 1805, the following prime ministers were alive: Grafton , Shelburne, Portland , Pitt , Addington , Lord Grenville , Perceval , Liverpool , Canning , Goderich , Wellington , Grey , Melbourne , Peel , Lord John Russell , Lord Derby , Lord Aberdeen , Lord Palmerston and Disraeli.
* Since the appointment of Anthony Eden on 6 April 1955 (a period of 71 years, 119 days), there have been at least three prime ministers living, and since the appointment of Lord Salisbury on 23 June 1885 (a period of 141 years, 41 days), there have been at least 2 prime ministers living.
